research.title: Evaluating transparency in AI/ML model characteristics for FDA-reviewed medical devices
research.paperTitle: Evaluating transparency in AI/ML model characteristics for FDA-reviewed medical devices
research.excerpt: Clear model and dataset documentation is essential for interpreting an AI device’s reported performance.
research.html:
What the paper explores

This study assessed transparency in publicly available FDA device summaries across model-development and performance-reporting categories. Using an AI Characteristics Transparency Reporting score, the authors found limited disclosure across many of the assessed characteristics, despite modest improvement after the period associated with good machine learning practice principles.

How to interpret the evidence

The score describes public reporting, not the complete regulatory submission or the inherent quality of every model. Missing public information should not be treated as proof that a study was not performed.

Questions for MedTech teams

Document model scope, data provenance, evaluation methods and limitations in a traceable form that connects technical work with clinical and regulatory communication.

research.paperTitle: Performance of Rapid Antigen Tests to Detect Symptomatic and Asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 Infection : A Prospective Cohort Study
research.excerpt: Why the timing and repetition of an antigen test matter as much as its single-test sensitivity.
research.html:
What the paper explores

This prospective US cohort paired home antigen testing with molecular testing every 48 hours. Performance differed by symptom status, and repeat testing improved detection. The study treats a sequence of tests as an evaluation strategy, rather than assuming one negative result answers the clinical question.

How to interpret the evidence

The tested interval was 48 hours. The results do not establish performance for shorter intervals, other products or every later viral variant.

Questions for MedTech teams

For an IVD study, define the intended population, testing schedule and interpretation of repeated results before selecting performance endpoints.

research.excerpt: Self-sampling, symptoms and the reason for testing can change the performance measured in a diagnostic study.
research.html:
What the paper explores

The investigators evaluated unsupervised rapid antigen self-tests among symptomatic people during the Omicron period in the Netherlands. Results varied with the sampling approach and with whether participants were already confirming a positive self-test. That recruitment context is an important part of interpreting the reported sensitivity.

How to interpret the evidence

This was a diagnostic accuracy study in a particular epidemic and recruitment setting. Its results should not be transferred directly to a different population. A published correction is linked below; consult the corrected article before using exact values.

Questions for MedTech teams

Document who enters the study, why they seek testing and how specimens are collected. Those details help explain what a reported performance estimate actually represents.

research.excerpt: A study of close contacts illustrates why intended-use populations and testing time must be defined together.
research.html:
What the paper explores

This cross-sectional study assessed rapid antigen testing in asymptomatic and presymptomatic close contacts of people with confirmed infection. Diagnostic sensitivity changed when the analysis considered subsequent symptoms or used a viral-load threshold as a proxy for infectiousness.

How to interpret the evidence

A viral-load threshold is a proxy, not a direct measurement of transmission. Findings from close contacts tested at a defined point after exposure do not establish accuracy for every screening use.

Questions for MedTech teams

Plan separate analyses for the intended clinical question. Detecting any infection and identifying a high viral-load subset are different evaluation targets.

The Test Us At Home study used digital recruitment and remote participation to evaluate repeated antigen testing. This is a study-design and implementation report. Operational feasibility does not by itself prove the performance of a new test, or guarantee that the same approach suits another population.

Remote clinical operations still need clear instructions, sample logistics, traceable data and reliable follow-up. Treat these as parts of the evidence plan from the start.

research.html:
What the paper explores

The Diverse Dermatology Images study assembled a curated, pathology-confirmed image dataset with varied skin tones and conditions. The authors found weaknesses in existing dermatology AI models, especially on darker skin tones and less common diseases. They also examined the effect of fine-tuning on representative data.

How to interpret the evidence

A curated dataset is an important evaluation tool, but it is not a substitute for prospective evidence in the intended clinical workflow. Findings depend on the models and image set examined.

Questions for MedTech teams

Plan representative data collection and subgroup evaluation before deployment. Aggregate accuracy can hide a product’s most consequential failure modes.

What the paper explores

CancerSEEK combined circulating protein measurements with cell-free DNA mutation analysis. The study evaluated patients with already diagnosed, nonmetastatic cancers and healthy controls, and explored whether positive results could narrow the likely anatomical origin of the cancer.

How to interpret the evidence

Performance in known cases and healthy controls cannot establish screening performance in an unselected population. Clinical benefit, downstream investigation and the consequences of false positives require separate evidence.

Questions for MedTech teams

For a new IVD, align the population and reference method with the proposed clinical use. The paper’s Johns Hopkins academic affiliations do not imply an affiliation with Hopkins MedTech.

This prospective cohort evaluated the feasibility of a multicancer early detection blood test in adults without signs or symptoms of cancer. A positive signal initiated diagnostic assessment. The investigators measured the time and testing needed to reach a diagnostic resolution, including the experience of people with false-positive results.

A convenience cohort and feasibility outcomes do not establish a mortality benefit or settle the clinical utility of population screening. The cohort’s composition also matters when considering generalizability.

Diagnostic evidence planning should include the pathway after the result: referrals, confirmatory procedures, time to resolution and potential harms.

A wider scientific toolkit

The 2024 Chemistry Nobel recognized David Baker’s computational protein design and Demis Hassabis and John Jumper’s protein-structure prediction. From discovery to a defined question

Our editorial interpretation is that increasingly capable models make the research question more important: what is being predicted, against which reference, and for whom? Scientific recognition does not establish the performance of a particular diagnostic test or medical AI system.

Before incorporating a model into a study, specify its intended role, record the origin of its inputs and separate exploratory predictions from prospectively evaluated endpoints. These are planning considerations, not findings of the Nobel-recognized work.

The transition dates

Regulation (EU) 2024/1860 extends eligible legacy-device transitions to 31 December 2027 for IVDD-certified and class D devices; 31 December 2028 for class C; and 31 December 2029 for class B and class A sterile. Eligibility is conditional, including continued IVDD compliance, no significant design or intended-purpose change, acceptable risk, an IVDR quality system by 26 May 2025, and timely notified-body application and agreement.

A separate database milestone

The European Commission states that four EUDAMED modules became mandatory on 28 May 2026: actor registration, UDI/device registration, notified bodies/certificates, and market surveillance. Responsibilities differ by actor; the market-surveillance module concerns authorities.

Turn dates into responsibilities

A useful planning exercise is to maintain separate records for transition eligibility and database obligations. Assign an owner, supporting evidence and a review date to each relevant requirement. A future transition end date should not be interpreted as permission to postpone every earlier obligation.

The research question

Tesfamarian and colleagues describe two- and three-dimensional skin models incorporating regional and age-related morphology. Their 2025 preprint simulates transdermal transport for 50 chemicals and examines the influence of diffusion, partitioning and molecular properties.

Simulation is conditional evidence

A model’s prediction depends on its geometry, parameter values, boundary conditions and assumptions. It is not itself a measurement from a clinical population. Findings from a particular formulation or modeled skin region should not be assumed to transfer to another without evaluation.

A useful role in research

Our editorial interpretation is that such models can help formulate experimental questions and identify influential parameters. A clear comparison with independent experimental data is still needed before treating a prediction as evidence for a defined application.

insights.excerpt: A large hospital study illustrates why intended users, symptoms and study setting belong beside every performance estimate.
insights.html:
What was studied

Wagenhäuser and colleagues compared rapid antigen tests with RT-qPCR at a single German tertiary-care hospital between November 2020 and June 2023. Across 78,798 paired results, overall sensitivity was 34.5% and specificity was 99.6%. Higher viral load and typical COVID-19 symptoms were associated with a positive antigen result among infected individuals.

What the estimate does not say

The findings describe the tests, population and screening use in this study. They are not a universal sensitivity estimate for every rapid antigen product, symptomatic setting or specimen workflow. The authors associated the decline over time primarily with a changing symptom profile.

Implication for study planning

Our editorial takeaway is to define the intended population before choosing a performance target. Record symptoms, timing, comparator, specimen procedures and subgroup analyses so that the result can be interpreted in the context of intended use.

What the review covers

The 2023 Pharmaceutics review, “Current Advances in Lipid Nanosystems Intended for Topical and Transdermal Drug Delivery Applications,” considers skin structure, nanoparticle penetration routes and factors affecting delivery. Its abstract identifies particle size, surface charge and formulation components among the variables that need to be understood and controlled.

Avoid a universal size rule

HMC’s LinkedIn discussion uses particle size to explore possible delivery routes. The editorial takeaway is more qualified: a size measurement on its own does not establish where a formulation will travel or how much active substance will be delivered. Skin condition, carrier composition and the distinction between topical and transdermal delivery matter.

Make the endpoint explicit

A research plan should distinguish material retained at the surface, deposited in a follicle, delivered into skin, and transported across it. These are different outcomes. Evidence for one should not silently become a claim for another.

What changed

FDA’s final order, published on 25 March 2026 and effective 24 April 2026, moved optical diagnostic devices for melanoma and electrical impedance spectrometers from class III to class II with special controls. Our editorial suggestion is to document the target users, patients, output and role in the care pathway before translating a classification decision into study requirements. Three distinct research settings

A 2026 skin-tone dataset preprint examines labeling and benchmarking. A 2023 microneedle study compares machine-learning approaches for drug-permeation prediction and identifies drug loading, permeation time and microneedle surface area as influential variables. A September 2026 preprint compares three multimodal AI models with three dermatologists using patient-captured images; results depend on the metric, and model confidence is not consistently well calibrated.

Keep the claims attached to the task

These studies do not measure the same capability. Predicting permeation is different from classifying skin tone or interpreting a lesion image. High performance in one dataset does not establish reliability across a new population, acquisition method or intended use.

Research and regulation answer different questions

The FDA’s 2026 melanoma-device order concerns specific adjunctive device types. It does not validate the research systems discussed here. Our editorial recommendation is to describe each model through its task, reference standard, evaluation population and limitations before discussing practical use.

insights.title: Skin-tone auditing starts with the measurement
insights.excerpt: Before interpreting model agreement, establish what the labels and the scoring rule mean.
insights.html:
A dataset and a labeling problem

The 2026 preprint “Large-Scale Dataset and Benchmark for Skin Tone Classification in the Wild” reports 42,313 images from 3,564 individuals with ten-category Monk Skin Tone annotations. It explores classification and benchmark design, including dataset imbalance and leakage concerns.

Agreement depends on the rule

Exact-category agreement and agreement within one adjacent category answer different questions. A model can perform differently under these metrics without any change to its predictions. Human annotation variability is therefore part of interpreting a score, but it should not be described as a mathematically fixed ceiling on all future systems.

An editorial checklist for evaluation

Record the scale, annotation procedure, image conditions, participant overlap and subgroup distribution. Separate person-level data splits from image-level splits, and report the metric alongside the result. A skin-tone benchmark alone cannot establish diagnostic accuracy, fairness across every clinical use, or fitness for a medical-device claim.

sections.title: Intended Role
paragraphs: An early-stage concept needs a defensible answer to who would pay, how much, and through which channel. This role builds that answer from public evidence. You will size the market from the bottom up, map competitors and channels, and assess which commercialization paths are realistic given regulatory and cost constraints. The emphasis is on traceable assumptions, not on optimistic totals.

sections.title: Principal Duties
paragraphs: – Build bottom-up market sizing models where each assumption is stated, sourced, and independently adjustable.
– Map the competing products across consumer apps, clinical tools, device makers, and skincare brands.
– Research channel options such as direct to consumer, clinic and dermatology partnerships, retail, and licensing.
– Analyze pricing and business models in comparable products, including subscription, per-use, and bundled offers.
– Summarize how regulatory positioning, wellness versus medical, changes the cost and speed of each route.
– Maintain a sourced research log so any number in a deck can be traced back to its origin within one click.
– Use approved AI tools to accelerate research and drafting, then verify every figure against the primary source.

sections.title: Example Assignments
paragraphs: Assignments depend on active studies, authorized data access, and the internship timeline. Examples may include: – A bottom-up market sizing model with a sensitivity analysis on the three assumptions that matter most
– A competitor and sales-channel comparison with positioning, pricing, and claim comparisons
– A commercialization pathway assessment comparing routes on cost, speed, evidence burden, and risk

sections.title: Your First Two Weeks
paragraphs: – Assemble the source list: industry data, filings, pricing pages, and public health statistics.
– Build the first bottom-up sizing model with every assumption stated and sourced.
– Map ten comparable products by positioning, price, channel, and claims made.
– Write the one-page question list: what we must know before choosing a commercial route.

sections.title: About Hopkins Medtech
paragraphs: Hopkins MedTech Group LLC is a U.S. company working in medical technology and in vitro diagnostics. Its work covers clinical performance studies, protocol development and site coordination, data review and quality assurance, and regulatory support for United States and European pathways. The group is also exploring AI and digital health through an early-stage research initiative in facial and skin analysis.

sections.title: Required Qualifications
paragraphs: – Currently pursuing, or recently completed, a degree in business, economics, public health, health administration, marketing, or a related field, or able to show equivalent self-study or project work.
– Solid spreadsheet skills, including building a model whose assumptions someone else can change and re-run.
– Strong written English and the ability to make a structured, evidence-based argument in a short document.
– Rigorous sourcing habits, including the willingness to label an estimate as an estimate.
– Comfort researching regulated healthcare markets where claims and evidence requirements shape economics.
– No prior market research, consulting, or professional internship experience is required.

sections.title: Preferred Qualifications
paragraphs: Not screening criteria. Coursework, labs, personal projects, and self- study all count as evidence. – A course or competition project involving market sizing, a business case, or a pitch
– Exposure to healthcare reimbursement, consumer health markets, or dermatology and skincare categories
– Familiarity with research sources such as industry reports, company filings, or public health statistics

sections.title: What You Will Gain
paragraphs: – Learn to size a market from the bottom up, where every assumption has to survive a question.
– Understand how regulatory positioning changes the economics of a health product.
– Practice building analysis that an executive can challenge line by line and still trust.
– Leave with a sourced market model and pathway assessment you can defend in an interview.

sections.title: Deliverables
paragraphs: – A sourced market sizing model with documented assumptions and sensitivity ranges
– A competitor and sales-channel comparison with pricing and positioning comparisons
– A commercialization pathway memo with a recommendation and its stated conditions

sections.title: Supervision And Evaluation
paragraphs: Interns report to a named project lead, meet on a set weekly cadence, and receive written feedback on each deliverable. Work is evaluated on accuracy and traceability of sources, documentation quality, responsiveness to feedback, judgment about what to escalate, and disciplined use of approved AI tools. We expect steady learning and iteration rather than polished perfection on the first day.

sections.title: What We Do Not Expect
paragraphs: – Prior internship experience, or a name-brand employer on your CV.
– Knowing the regulations, tools, or vocabulary before you start; the terms box above is where most people begin.
– Certainty. Saying what the evidence does not support is treated as a strength, not a gap.

sections.title: Application And Selection
paragraphs: Candidates are referred through our education partners. An application is a CV plus a short note naming the track you want and one project from this document you would like to work on, and why. First-round interviews are with the project lead who would supervise the work, not with a screening panel.

sections.title: Data Handling, Privacy, And Responsible Ai
paragraphs: Interns work only with data and documents they have been explicitly authorized to access. Patient-identifiable information, study data, client- confidential files, and proprietary materials must never be uploaded to public or unapproved AI services, shared outside the project team, or stored on personal accounts or devices. AI tools may be used only

where the project lead has approved them for that task, and all AI- assisted work must be independently verified before it enters any deliverable. The intern and the project lead remain accountable for the final result.

sections.title: Equal Opportunity & Educational Nature
paragraphs: Hopkins MedTech Group LLC provides equal internship and employment opportunities without regard to race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, national origin, age, disability, veteran status, or any other legally protected characteristic. Internships are educational in nature; interns do not provide medical advice, make regulatory determinations, or represent the company to any health authority, client, or study site. The AI and digital health initiative described here is early-stage research, not a cleared, approved, or clinically validated product. Assignments, data access, duration, and supervision are confirmed in the final project description.
